### custom functions to implement kPCA reconstructions
plot_digit <- function(pixels){
  image(1:28, 1:28, t(matrix(pixels,nrow = 28,byrow = T))[,28:1], 
        xaxt='n', yaxt='n', xaxs = 'i',yaxs = 'i',xlab = '', ylab = '')
}

K <- function(x,y,sigma){
  m <- nrow(x)
  n <- nrow(y)
  if (is.null(m)){
    m <- 1; 
    sx2 <-sum(x^2)
    x <- as.matrix(x,nrow = 1)
    } else {
    sx2 <- rowSums(x^2)
  }
  if (is.null(n)){
    n <- 1; 
    sy2 <- sum(y^2)
    y <- as.matrix(y, ncol = 1)
    } else {
    sy2 <- rowSums(y^2)
    y <- t(y)
  }
  A <- matrix(rep(sx2,n), nrow = m, ncol = n, byrow = F)
  B <- matrix(rep(sy2,m), nrow = m, ncol = n, byrow = T)
  return(exp(-sigma*(A+B-2* x %*% y)))
}

reconstruct <- function(samples, kpca_fit, n_comp, tol = 1e-4, max_iter = 1e3){
  rec <- as.matrix(samples)
  n <- nrow(kpca_fit@pcv)
  K.data <- K(kpca_fit@xmatrix,kpca_fit@xmatrix,
         sigma=kpca_fit@kernelf@kpar$sigma)
  H <- diag(rep(1,n)) - matrix(1/n,n,n)
  HKH.eig <- eigen(H %*% K.data %*% H)
  USinv <- HKH.eig$vectors[,1:n_comp] %*% diag(HKH.eig$values[1:n_comp]^-0.5)
  
  for (j in 1:nrow(rec)){
    kx <- K(kpca_fit@xmatrix, rec[j,], sigma=kpca_fit@kernelf@kpar$sigma)
    # gam <- kpca_fit@pcv[,1:n_comp] %*% diag(kpca_fit@eig[1:n_comp]^-2) %*% t(kpca_fit@pcv[,1:n_comp]) %*% (kx-rowSums(HKH)/n)
    # gam <- kpca_fit@pcv[,1:n_comp] %*% t(kpca_fit@pcv[,1:n_comp]) %*% kx
    gam <- USinv %*% t(USinv) %*% H %*% (kx-rowSums(K.data)/n)
    # gam <- USinv %*% t(USinv) %*% H %*% kx
    weights <- 1/n + gam - sum(gam)
    # weights <- gam
    
    out <- colMeans(kpca_fit@xmatrix)
    iter <- 0
    dif = Inf
    while(iter < max_iter && dif > tol){
      old <- out
      new_weight <- weights*as.vector(K(kpca_fit@xmatrix,old,sigma=kpca_fit@kernelf@kpar$sigma))
      out <- t(new_weight) %*% kpca_fit@xmatrix / sum(new_weight)
      dif <- sum((old-out)^2)
      # print(iter)
      # print(dif)
      iter <- iter+1
    }
    rec[j,] <- out
  }
  return(rec)
}

## Instructions {.tabset}
This assignment covers Multidimensional Scaling, kernel PCA, and manifold theory through a mixture of theory and coding.  You will need the file *pset4.Rdata* available on Canvas.  The commands for loading the data assume this file, *pset4-2024.Rmd*, and the Rdata file are in the same folder.

You can use the command *cmdscale(d, k , eig = FALSE)* to compute the solution to the classical scaling problem. Here $d$ is a matrix of distances, $k$ is the dimension of the desired configuration, and the option *eig=TRUE* may be added so that eigenvalues are also reported.

For metric MDS, use the command *sammon(d, k, trace = FALSE)* for metric MDS using Sammon's Stress.  Here $d$ is a matrix of distances, $k$ is the dimension of the desired configuration, and the option *trace = FALSE* stops reporting of the stress over iterations of the algorithm.

Given a data matrix, all pairwise distances can be calculated using the command *dist(x)* where $x$ is the data matrix. The default method is the Euclidean distance. All of the above MDS commands require a matrix of distances or variable of type *dist* given by the output of the *dist()* function.

You can use the code *out <- kpca(data,kernel = "kernelname", kpar = list("param_name" = param_value))* to implement kernel PCA. The kernel PCA scores can be accessed via *out@rotated* and the variances via *out@eig*.

Complete the following questions and submit your solutions as a *pdf* by 11:59 PM on October 31st.

### Problem 2

a. Suppose we have $d$-dimensional data $\vec{x}_1,\dots,\vec{x}_N$ from which we compute, the sample mean $\bar{x}$, principal component loadings which are the columns of ${\bf W} \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$, the principal component variances $\lambda_1 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_d$, and principal component scores $${\bf Y} = {\bf (H X) W} = \begin{bmatrix} \vec{x}_1^T - \bar{x}^T \\ \vdots \\ \vec{x}_N^T - \bar{x}^T \end{bmatrix} {\bf W}.$$  Give a formula for the principal component scores $\vec{z}_0$ of $\vec{x}_0$ based on the sample mean and loadings obtained from our original data.

b. In class, we showed how to compute the kernel principal component scores from an uncentered kernel matrix ${\bf K}$. We compute the eigendecomposition of ${\bf HKH} = {\bf \hat{U} S^2 \hat{U}}^T$ from which we get kernel PC scores ${\bf \hat{U} S}$, Suppose we have the inner product vector $$\vec{k}_0 = \left[k(\vec{x}_1,\vec{x}_0), \dots, k(\vec{x}_N,\vec{x}_0)\right]^T,$$ containing the $N$ feature vector inner-products between a new point $\vec{x}_0$ and each of the $\vec{x}_i$ in our original dataset. Show that the (centered) projections of $\vec{x}_0$ onto the kernel principal component loadings are given by $$\vec{z}_0 = {\bf S}^{-1}{\bf U}^T{\bf H}\left[\vec{k}_0 - \frac{1}{N} {\bf K}\vec{1}_N\right].$$

#### Problem 3

#### Problem 6 (UL in Action) 

As discussed in class, one application of kernel PCA is for denoising data.  In this problem, we'll explore how kPCA reconstructions can be used to tune kernel PCA and denoise data.  The function **recons(sample, kpca_fit, n_comp)** finds the reconstruction for sample point(s), *samples*, given a kernel pca fit, *kpca\_fit* using a specific number of component, *n\_comp*.

For this problem, we'll be working with noisy versions of the MNIST dataset. One example is shown below.

```{r, fig.align='center',fig.cap="1st noisy image in the training set"}
plot_digit(noisy_digits_train[1,])
```
